_note: Things rovers can scavenge. workHours = Mars hours working on site per trip. loads = trips before it's used up; yield is per trip. clearsTile = the tile becomes buildable afterwards. Metal and regolith are scavenged on purpose: oxygen, water and food come from buildings.

nodes.name: Iron Meteorite
nodes.description: A chunk of iron and nickel from space, lying on the surface.
nodes.scienceNote: Iron meteorites are tough enough to survive the fall through Mars's thin air. NASA's Opportunity rover found one in 2005, the first meteorite ever identified on another planet.

nodes.name: Lander Wreckage
nodes.description: Leftover hardware from your own landing.
nodes.scienceNote: Every Mars landing leaves hardware behind: heat shield, parachute, back shell and descent stage. Reusing it saves shipping new metal all the way from Earth.

nodes.name: Iron Ore (Hematite)
nodes.description: Iron-rich rock. Takes a while to process into usable metal.
nodes.scienceNote: Hematite is an iron oxide mineral. Turning ore into metal takes much more work than grabbing a meteorite that's already metal.

nodes.name: Boulder
nodes.description: Clear it to make room, and bring back broken rock as regolith for radiation shielding.
nodes.scienceNote: Robots clear rocks so astronauts spend less time outside, where they'd soak up more radiation.
